title: Polarisation as evidence of transverse waves
prior_knowledge_summary: Electromagnetic waves are transverse and the principal electromagnetic regions can be ordered by wavelength or frequency.
In a transverse wave, displacement is perpendicular to energy transfer; in a longitudinal wave, oscillations are parallel to energy transfer.
new_learning: Relate plane polarisation to restriction of transverse oscillations.
Explain why longitudinal waves cannot be polarised in this sense.

visual_planning.reason: Seven distinct sketches make three-dimensional oscillation directions and filter-axis reasoning visible without duplicating a scene.

blocks.heading: A filter that reveals a hidden direction
content: Two identical-looking sheets are placed in a light beam. Turning one sheet changes the transmitted light, even though the beam still travels straight ahead. What hidden direction can the sheet detect?
The answer is not the direction of travel. It is the direction in which the transverse wave oscillates.

figure.purpose: Create the puzzle of rotation-dependent transmission.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful teacher sketch. Show a torch beam passing through two simple filter frames, with the second frame partly rotated and a screen changing brightness. Add a question mark beside a small axis marker. Do not show an intensity formula or answer labels.
figure.alt_text: A light beam passes through two filter frames while one rotates and the screen brightness changes.

blocks.heading: Transverse motion has room for many directions
content: Recall the accepted definition: a transverse wave is a wave in which the displacement of particles is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
If the wave travels forward, its oscillation may be vertical, horizontal or along another sideways direction. All these directions remain perpendicular to travel.
That freedom is what a polarising filter can sort.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: a wave in which the displacement of particles is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer

figure.purpose: Separate propagation direction from possible transverse oscillation directions.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful teacher sketch. Draw one forward energy-transfer arrow and a sparse fan of sideways oscillation arrows in the plane perpendicular to it. Highlight vertical and horizontal as two examples.
figure.alt_text: A forward energy-transfer arrow is perpendicular to several possible sideways oscillation directions.

blocks.heading: Plane polarisation restricts the oscillation
content: An unpolarised transverse electromagnetic wave contains oscillations in many directions perpendicular to travel.
After a suitable polarising filter, the transmitted oscillations are restricted to one direction. The wave is plane polarised.
The plane of polarisation contains both that single oscillation direction and the direction of travel. The filter transmission axis marks the allowed oscillation direction.

figure.purpose: Show the before-and-after restriction produced by a polarising filter.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful teacher sequence. Before the filter, draw several sparse transverse oscillation arrows around the beam. On the filter, draw one vertical transmission axis. After it, draw only vertical oscillation arrows. Label travel direction and allowed direction.
figure.alt_text: Many transverse oscillation directions enter a filter and one allowed direction leaves.

blocks.heading: Read the direction, not the drawing style
content: Imagine a horizontally plane-polarised microwave travelling towards a receiver. Its field oscillation is horizontal while energy travels towards the receiver.

A filter with a horizontal transmission axis is aligned with that oscillation. Turning the axis away changes how much passes, but this lesson only identifies the directions. The quantitative rule comes next.
A reliable description names the propagation direction, then names the single perpendicular oscillation direction.

figure.purpose: Model a complete directional description of a plane-polarised wave.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper annotated direction sketch. Draw a microwave travelling right, horizontal double-headed oscillation arrows, and a front-view filter with a horizontal transmission axis. Keep the transmitted brightness qualitative and omit angles or formulas.
figure.alt_text: A microwave travels right while oscillating horizontally through a horizontally aligned filter.

blocks.heading: Why longitudinal waves fail the test
content: In a longitudinal wave, the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. There is no family of different sideways oscillation directions for a filter to select.

For sound in air, compressions and rarefactions move along the same line as the wave travels. Rotating a filter around that line cannot restrict the motion to one transverse direction because the motion is not transverse.
So sound waves in air cannot be plane polarised in this sense. This comparison makes polarisation evidence that a wave is transverse.

figure.purpose: Contrast selectable transverse directions with longitudinal motion along travel.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper split comparison. Left: transverse wave with a forward arrow and two possible sideways oscillation directions. Right: longitudinal compression sketch with particle motion arrows along travel. Put a rotating filter outline around each beam path and a small tick only on the transverse side.
figure.alt_text: Transverse oscillations offer sideways directions to select, while longitudinal motion stays along the travel direction.

blocks.heading: Polarised does not mean the wave travels in one direction
content: It is reasonable to hear restricted direction and think that the beam itself has been forced onto one path. The words sound similar.
Polarisation does not restrict the direction of travel. It restricts the direction of oscillation while the wave continues to propagate forward.

Another trap is saying that a longitudinal wave has only one oscillation direction, so it must already be polarised. That direction is parallel to travel, not one selected direction perpendicular to travel, so it is not plane polarisation.

figure.purpose: Correct confusion between propagation direction and oscillation direction.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper error clinic. Cross out a bent beam labelled travel restricted. Beside it, keep a straight propagation arrow and show many transverse arrows becoming one transverse direction. Add a longitudinal compression row with parallel arrows and a not-polarised note.
figure.alt_text: Polarisation leaves travel direction unchanged and restricts only transverse oscillation direction.

blocks.heading: A three-step polarisation test
content: First identify the direction of energy transfer. Next identify the direction or directions of oscillation.

If the oscillations are perpendicular to travel, they can be restricted to one direction and the wave can be plane polarised. If oscillations are parallel to travel, this kind of polarisation is impossible.
Therefore successful plane polarisation is evidence that a wave is transverse. The next lesson will quantify transmission when the polariser axis is rotated.

figure.purpose: Consolidate the classification and explanation route.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper decision flow: find travel direction, compare oscillation direction, branch perpendicular to can be plane polarised and parallel to cannot be plane polarised in this sense. End the first branch at evidence of transverse wave. No intensity law.
figure.alt_text: A decision flow links perpendicular oscillations to possible plane polarisation and transverse-wave evidence.

concepts_taught: restriction of transverse oscillations to one direction
polarisation as evidence of transverse waves
longitudinal waves cannot be plane polarised in this sense
misconceptions_addressed: Polarisation restricts the direction of wave travel.
A longitudinal wave is already polarised because it has one oscillation direction.
A polarising filter changes a transverse wave into a longitudinal wave.
next_lesson_can_assume: Describe plane polarisation as restriction of transverse oscillations to one direction.
Identify the transmission axis as the allowed oscillation direction.
Explain why longitudinal waves cannot be plane polarised in this sense.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Calculate intensity after one or more polarising filters.
Assume that the first polariser halves unpolarised-light intensity.
